85.title: Paul in Athens (Acts 17:16–34)
85.hook: he quotes their own poets: in him we live and move and have our being
85.howItsDone: Christians often point to Paul's speech on the Areopagus as a model for speaking respectfully with people of other views. The line 'in him we live, and move, and have our being' is widely used in prayers and hymns.

segments.voice: Yesterday, purple cloth: Lydia the seller of purple, and the jailer, and two men singing in the stocks.

Where do you start with someone who sees the world differently, at a wedding or in a comment thread? Most of us start with where they're wrong. Paul is in Athens, the ancient world's city of ideas, alone, waiting for his friends. He walks the streets, deeply stirred: the city is full of statues and altars to many gods, and he's a Jew who worships one. He talks in the synagogue and the marketplace with anyone who'll listen, Stoic and Epicurean philosophers among them. Some call him a babbler. Others are curious. They take him to the Areopagus, the council's hill, and say: tell us this new thing.
screen: `WHERE DO YOU START?` → `A CITY OF IDEAS.` → `UP TO THE AREOPAGUS.`

segments.voice: Paul begins with a compliment: I see you're a very religious people. Walking around, he says, I found an altar inscribed, in the King James Bible: "TO THE UNKNOWN GOD." He doesn't mock it; he starts from it. The one you honor without knowing is the one I proclaim: the God who made the world, who doesn't live in buildings made by hands, and isn't far from any of us. Then, unexpectedly for a traveling Jewish teacher, he quotes their own poets: "For in him we live, and move, and have our being; as certain also of your own poets have said, For we are also his offspring." The second line is from the Greek poet Aratus, about three centuries earlier; the first is often credited to another, Epimenides, though scholars aren't sure. Either way, Paul stands on their hill and speaks their language. Then he reaches his center: a day of judgment, and a man raised from the dead. That's where the room splits: at the resurrection, some laugh. Others say, politely, we'll hear you again. A few believe, and Luke names two: Dionysius, a council member, and a woman, Damaris. Christians have long pointed to this speech as a way to talk across a gap: start with what's good and true in the other person's world, honor it, then say plainly what you believe. A line Paul borrowed from Greek poets has been prayed and sung by Christians ever since. In him we live.

segments.voice: Picture someone with a view you don't share, a politics, a faith, a way of raising kids or spending money, and look for their altar to the unknown god: the thing they're reaching for that you can honor, like safety, fairness, freedom, or love for their family. Name it kindly; you don't have to agree, just find the good. If you pray, you can pray for them.

86.title: The shipwreck (Acts 27–28)
86.hook: two weeks of storm, Paul breaks bread on deck, 276 swim to Malta, and a viper bites harmlessly
86.howItsDone: Many Christians give thanks before meals, as Paul does on the deck. In Malta, Paul's shipwreck is remembered every February 10 with a public holiday and feast, and Maltese tradition traces the island's faith to it.

segments.voice: Yesterday, unknown god: Paul at the altar in Athens, quoting the poets on their own hill.

Some weeks are all storm, and you can't see the sky. Now board a cargo ship in the Mediterranean, late in the sailing season. Paul is aboard as a prisoner, not a passenger, taken to Rome for trial under a Roman officer named Julius. Paul warns it's too late in the year to sail. Nobody listens. Then a violent wind sweeps off Crete; the ship is caught and can't turn into it. They lash ropes around the hull to hold it together, throw the cargo overboard, then the ship's gear. Day after day, no sun, no stars. Luke, writing as we, as if aboard, says all hope that we should be saved was taken away.
screen: `A PRISONER ON A CARGO SHIP.` → `THE WIND OFF CRETE.` → `NO SUN, NO STARS.`

segments.voice: Paul stands among the exhausted crew: in the King James Bible, "And now I exhort you to be of good cheer: for there shall be no loss of any man's life among you, but of the ship." An angel stood by me last night, he says. Again: "Wherefore, sirs, be of good cheer: for I believe God." Be of good cheer is the King James wording; the Greek means something like be good-spirited. Take heart. On the fourteenth night they sense land. Some sailors try to slip away in the lifeboat, and are stopped. Before dawn, everyone starving and terrified, Paul does something ordinary: tells them to eat. Two weeks without a real meal, he says; this is for your health. Then "he took bread, and gave thanks to God in presence of them all: and when he had broken it, he began to eat." Took, gave thanks, broke: Luke's words for anamnesis, now on a storm-battered deck, among soldiers, sailors and prisoners. All take heart and eat; Luke counts two hundred and seventy-six people. At daybreak the ship runs aground and breaks apart. Swimmers jump first; the rest float in on planks. Every one reaches the shore. It's Malta; the islanders build a fire in the cold rain. A viper comes out of the firewood and fastens onto Paul's hand. The locals decide he must be a murderer. He shakes it into the fire, nothing happens, and they change their minds: he must be a god.
screen: `BE OF GOOD CHEER.` · `THIS IS FOR YOUR HEALTH.` · `HE TOOK BREAD, AND GAVE THANKS.` · `276, ALL SAFE TO LAND.` · then, large: `TAKE HEART.`

segments.voice: If you have something near, bread, a cracker, fruit, a cup of tea, hold it before you eat; if not, picture it. If you pray, give thanks for it, as Paul did; if not, notice where it came from, and how many hands it passed through. Then eat slowly, like someone who hasn't eaten in a while, and let it steady you, one bite at a time.

87.title: The letters as letters
87.hook: Paul's letters are real post: greetings, travel plans, and a list of friends' names (Romans 16)
87.howItsDone: In Catholic, Orthodox, Anglican, Lutheran and other churches, a reading from one of the New Testament letters, often called the Epistle, is read aloud at Sunday worship, the way the letters were first heard by the churches they were sent to.

segments.voice: Yesterday, the shipwreck: bread broken on a storm-battered deck, and everyone safe on Malta.

When did a real letter last land in your mailbox? Paper, not email: maybe a card from a grandparent, with the news, a little advice, and a list at the end: say hi to your mom, love to the kids. A whole run of New Testament books carry Paul's name, and they aren't essays or sermons. They're letters. Real mail, sent to real people in real cities: Rome, Corinth, Philippi, Thessalonica. Somebody carried them by hand, over roads and seas, and somebody read them aloud to a room full of people who knew the sender. At the very end of Romans is a page that's easy to skip.
screen: `A REAL LETTER, ON PAPER.` → `LETTERS WITH PAUL'S NAME.` → `READ TO THE VERY END.`

segments.voice: Today's word is epistle, from the Greek for something sent. Paul's letters follow the usual letter shape of his day: who it's from, who it's to, a greeting, grace and peace, then thanks, the business, travel plans, and hellos. Romans chapter sixteen is almost all hellos. It opens, in the King James Bible: "I commend unto you Phebe our sister, which is a servant of the church which is at Cenchrea." A note printed after Romans in the King James says the letter was sent by her. Then come more than twenty-five names. "Greet Priscilla and Aquila my helpers in Christ Jesus," a married couple who risked their necks for him, with a church meeting in their house. Andronicus and Junia, who were in prison with him. Tryphena and Tryphosa, who work hard. Rufus, and his mother, who was a mother to Paul too. Some he calls his kinsmen, fellow Jews; others have Greek and Latin names. Women and men, side by side. Near the end, a different voice breaks in: "I Tertius, who wrote this epistle, salute you in the Lord." Tertius is the scribe, writing as Paul speaks, adding his own hello. In other letters Paul takes the pen at the end and signs in his own big handwriting. In one he asks a friend to bring the coat he left behind, and his books. Why does it matter? The letters now read in church as scripture started as mail between friends. Christians read them as God's word, and they never stopped being letters, full of names.

segments.voice: Begin one real letter or card in your head, to someone who'd be surprised to hear from you. Start the way Paul did, with a greeting, then one specific thing you're grateful for about them, some ordinary news, and a list of names to say hello to. If you pray, you can pray for each name as it comes.
Epistle. From the Greek for something sent. Paul's letters: real mail, full of travel plans, a scribe's hello, and friends' names.

88.title: Philemon
88.hook: a short note asking a slave owner to receive Onesimus as a beloved brother
88.carry: no longer a servant, but a brother
88.howItsDone: Philemon is read in churches as a letter about reconciliation and about how faith changes relationships of power. It was also central in debates over slavery, when abolitionists and defenders of slavery read it in opposite ways.

segments.voice: Yesterday, epistle: Paul's letters as real mail, with a scribe's hello and a list of friends.

Ever written a note on someone else's behalf? A reference, or a text to smooth things over between friends: you choose every word; someone's future rides on it. Paul's letter to Philemon is that. It's one page, written from prison to Philemon, a believer with a church meeting in his home. It's about Onesimus, who is enslaved in Philemon's household, and has left. Somehow he found Paul in prison and became a believer. Now Paul sends him back carrying this letter. Philemon has the law on his side, and the power to punish. Everything depends on this page.
screen: `A NOTE FOR SOMEONE ELSE.` → `ONE PAGE, FROM PRISON.` → `ONESIMUS GOES BACK.`

segments.voice: Watch how Paul does it. He could order Philemon to do the right thing, but would rather appeal, for love's sake. He calls Onesimus my son, my very heart. He even jokes, since Onesimus means useful: "Which in time past was to thee unprofitable, but now profitable to thee and to me." Then the real request. Take him back, the King James Bible says, "Not now as a servant, but above a servant, a brother beloved." The Greek word translated servant is doulos: slave. Paul asks a slave owner to receive an enslaved man as a brother, in the flesh and in the Lord. Then he signs a blank check: "If he hath wronged thee, or oweth thee ought, put that on mine account." I, Paul, write this with my own hand: I will repay it. Near the end: knowing you'll do even more than I say. Now the honest part. The letter never says, in so many words, set him free. We don't know why Onesimus left, or what Philemon did next. The Bible is silent. Over the centuries, some Christians used Paul's letters to defend slavery, and others, including many who fought to end it, read this page as pointing the other way: once a man is your brother, how can he be your property? Later, a letter by Ignatius of Antioch names a bishop of Ephesus called Onesimus. Some wonder if it's the same man. Nobody knows. What's left is one page, where Paul puts his name on the line for someone with less power, and asks for a new word: brother.

segments.voice: Think of someone with less say than those around them: a new employee, a kid, someone who cleans the office after everyone leaves, someone whose English is still new. Picture putting in a word for them, as Paul did: a thank you said where the boss can hear, a good reference, something put on your account. If you pray, you can pray for them by name.

89.title: Love is patient (1 Corinthians 13)
89.hook: written to a quarrelling church, not a wedding: love is patient, kind, not puffed up
89.howItsDone: 1 Corinthians 13 is often read at Christian weddings and funerals, and churches also read it in Sunday worship. Some Christians learn its description of love by heart.

segments.voice: Yesterday, Philemon: one page asking for a new word. Your line was no longer a servant, but a brother.
screen: `NO LONGER A SERVANT, BUT A BROTHER.`

segments.voice: A wedding. Someone's cousin walks up to the microphone and reads: love is patient, love is kind. Everyone smiles at the couple. But that's not where it was first read. It was first read out loud to a church in Corinth, a busy port city in Greece, and that church was a mess. They'd split into fan clubs: I follow Paul, I follow Apollos, I follow Peter. Members were taking each other to court. At their shared meals, the wealthy ate first and the poor went hungry. And they competed over whose spiritual gifts were the most impressive. In the middle of a long letter to them, Paul stops arguing and writes this.
screen: `READ AT A WEDDING.` → `WRITTEN TO A MESS.` → `FAN CLUBS AND LAWSUITS.`

segments.voice: It starts with a warning to the show-offs, in the King James Bible: "Though I speak with the tongues of men and of angels, and have not charity, I am become as sounding brass, or a tinkling cymbal." Impressive, and just noise. Then the famous part: "Charity suffereth long, and is kind; charity envieth not; charity vaunteth not itself, is not puffed up." Charity, from the Latin caritas. The Greek word underneath is today's word: agape. It isn't the usual word for romance, or for friendship. Christian teachers describe it as the love that wills the good of the other, even when they're difficult. Christians say it's the love God has for the world. Now hear who it was for. Suffers long: to a church where people kept suing each other. Envies not: to people jealous of each other's gifts. Not puffed up: earlier in the same letter Paul had told them, knowledge puffs up, but love builds up. Line after line is a mirror held up to a quarreling room, a correction written with great tenderness. Love never fails, Paul goes on; everything else we have is partial: "For now we see through a glass, darkly." And he ends: "And now abideth faith, hope, charity, these three; but the greatest of these is charity." Churches still read it at weddings, and it belongs there too. But it was written for the hardest kind of love: loving people you're in the middle of a fight with. Which is also what a marriage needs.

90.title: What a saint is
90.hook: Paul calls every believer a saint; Catholics and Orthodox also honor holy people named by the church
90.howItsDone: Christians confess 'the communion of saints' in the Apostles' Creed. Catholics and Orthodox Christians ask the saints to pray for them and keep their feast days; Anglicans and Lutherans keep saints' calendars; many Protestants call every believer a saint.

segments.voice: Yesterday, agape: love that suffers long, written to a quarreling church. Your line was the greatest of these.

When you hear the word saint, what comes to mind? A stained-glass window, someone with a golden circle around their head. A city: San Francisco, Saint Louis, São Paulo. Or an eye-roll: well, I'm no saint. It means someone impossibly better than us. Now remember yesterday's church in Corinth: the fan clubs, the lawsuits, the rich eating first while the poor went hungry. How does Paul address his letter to them? To the church of God at Corinth, to them that are, as the King James puts it, called to be saints. That church. Those people. This week, the last of the stories, brings saints as real characters.
screen: `A GOLDEN CIRCLE, A CITY, AN EYE-ROLL.` → `I'M NO SAINT.` → `THE CORINTHIANS: CALLED TO BE SAINTS.`

segments.voice: The Greek word is hagios: holy, set apart, belonging to God. The Latin is sanctus, which gives us saint. In the New Testament it isn't a prize for the best people; it's a name for all of them. Paul opens his letter to Rome, in the King James Bible: "To all that be in Rome, beloved of God, called to be saints." To Philippi: to all the saints in Christ Jesus. Every believer, in every messy church, holy not because they'd earned it, but because God had claimed them. Ordinary people, made holy. Over the centuries, Christians also began to honor particular people whose lives shone: martyrs first, then teachers, monks, mothers, people who gave their lives to the poor. The churches differ here. Catholics recognize saints through a formal process called canonization, and ask the saints in heaven to pray for them, the way you'd ask a friend. Orthodox Christians honor saints in icons and hymns, and also ask their prayers. Anglicans and Lutherans keep calendars of saints' days and remember them as examples. Many other Protestants use the word mostly Paul's way, for every believer, and honor heroes of the faith without asking for their prayers. What all of them share is a line from the old creed: the communion of saints, God's people, living and dead, belonging together. The letter to the Hebrews pictures it as a stadium: "we also are compassed about with so great a cloud of witnesses." And many churches keep All Saints' Day, November first, for the famous and the forgotten alike.

91.title: Monica's tears
91.hook: a mother prays for years for her wayward son, Augustine, and a bishop tells her such tears won't be lost
91.howItsDone: Saint Monica is honored as a patron of mothers and of those who pray for loved ones who have drifted from faith. In the Catholic calendar her feast is August 27, the day before Saint Augustine's.

segments.voice: Yesterday, saint: in Paul's letters, every believer; later, holy lives remembered. Your line was ordinary people, made holy. Thirteen weeks on the path.

Some love keeps people up at night: loving someone who keeps making the choice you were afraid of. Rehearsing the conversation. Trying again, and watching it go badly again. Roman North Africa. A woman named Monica has a son who is brilliant, charming, ambitious and restless. His name is Augustine. He drifts from the faith she raised him in, throws himself into success, and into a way of life that breaks her heart. She weeps for him, prays for him, follows him around. Years go by. All of this survives because, years later, Augustine told the story himself, in a book addressed to God called the Confessions. And he doesn't spare himself.
screen: `AWAKE AT NIGHT.` → `A BRILLIANT, RESTLESS SON.` → `HE TOLD IT HIMSELF.`

segments.voice: At one point, Monica goes to a bishop and begs him to talk sense into her son. The bishop says no. He's not ready; leave him alone and keep praying; he'll find his own way. She won't take no. She keeps pleading, in floods of tears, until the bishop, a bit worn out, says: go your way, it cannot be that the son of these tears should perish. Augustine says his mother took that as if it had sounded from heaven. It didn't fix anything quickly. When Augustine decided to sail for Rome, he lied to her to slip away, and left her weeping on the shore. So she followed him, across the sea, all the way to Milan. There, finally, the road turned. Augustine was baptized at Easter by the bishop of Milan, Ambrose. Not long after, mother and son stood at a window in the port town of Ostia, near Rome, talking quietly about God, and Augustine describes the two of them touching something eternal for a moment. A few days later she fell ill and died, far from home, content. The son of those tears became a writer whom Christians in many churches still read, and churches honor Monica as a saint. Christians have held on to her story for the plainest reason: it says that years of tears, poured out for someone who seems not to be listening, are not wasted.

If you pray, bring them to God in whatever words you have, or none; if you don't, hold them in your mind with love, the way Monica did. Don't try to fix them; just don't let go.
